title: Old land, young nation
description: People reached the Americas thousands of years before the United States declared independence in 1776.

facts.text: The first Americans arrived about 25,000 to 15,000 years ago.

title: Turning points of US history
description: Independence (1776), the Constitution (1787), the Civil War (1861 to 1865) and the end of slavery (1865), Pearl Harbor (1941) and the Moon landing (1969).

facts.text: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
The US Constitution was written in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787 and signed on September 17, 1787.
The American Civil War (1861 to 1865) was fought between the United States and 11 Southern states that seceded and formed the Confederacy.
The 13th Amendment, ratified on December 6, 1865, abolished slavery in the United States.
Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941, brought the United States into World War II.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts became the first people to walk on the Moon.

title: From 13 colonies to 50 states
description: The Declaration spoke for 13 British colonies; Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959.

facts.text: The Declaration of Independence announced the separation of 13 British colonies in North America from Great Britain.
Hawaii became the 50th US state on August 21, 1959.

title: Across Beringia
description: During the last Ice Age, lower seas exposed Beringia, linking Siberia and Alaska; many scientists think people crossed it from East Asia, while others propose a coastal route by boat.

facts.text: During the last Ice Age, so much water was frozen in glaciers that sea levels fell by as much as about 400 feet, exposing Beringia, dry land where the Bering Strait's seafloor is now, linking Siberia and Alaska.
Many scientists think people crossed from East Asia into North America over the Bering Land Bridge, following the animals they hunted.
Some scientists propose that early peoples reached the Americas by boat or along a coastal route instead.

title: When the first Americans came
description: For decades Clovis (about 13,000 years ago) was thought to be first; Monte Verde, accepted in 1997, proved people came earlier; the White Sands footprints (about 21,000 to 23,000 years) are still debated.

facts.text: The Clovis culture is known for leaf-shaped, fluted stone spear points.
For decades, Clovis artifacts, about 13,000 years old, were the oldest known in the Americas, so many archaeologists thought the Clovis people were the first Americans.
Monte Verde, a campsite in southern Chile, shows people living there more than 14,000 years ago, earlier than Clovis.
Archaeologists broadly accepted Monte Verde's early date in 1997.
Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, have been dated to about 21,000 to 23,000 years ago.
Some archaeologists remain skeptical of the White Sands dates, arguing the dated material may seem older than it is.

title: Hundreds of languages
description: At European contact North America north of Mexico had about 300 languages; California alone showed more variety than all of Europe.

facts.text: At European contact, North America north of Mexico had about 300 distinct languages.
According to the linguist Edward Sapir, the languages of California alone showed more variety than all of Europe's.

title: Many ways of life
description: Anthropologists group Native North America into culture areas; some peoples hunted and gathered, others farmed; Northwest Coast peoples lived on abundant salmon; farming peoples planted corn, beans and squash together.

facts.text: Anthropologists group Native North America into culture areas, regions where similar ways of life occurred, such as the Northeast, the Plains, the Southwest and the Northwest Coast.
Many Native peoples lived by hunting and gathering, while others were farmers.
Northwest Coast peoples had abundant, reliable supplies of salmon and other fish, sea mammals and shellfish, and built large houses of timber planks.
Many farming peoples planted corn, beans and squash together; the Iroquois and the Cherokee called them the three sisters.
In a three sisters field, corn stalks support the beans, beans add nitrogen to the soil, and squash leaves shade out weeds and keep the soil moist.

title: Cahokia, a city north of Mexico
description: Cahokia, near St. Louis, flourished about 950 to 1350 on corn farming, held perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people around 1100, and declined probably through environmental damage.

facts.text: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was the largest urban center north of Mexico and flourished from about 950 to 1350.
Most people at Cahokia were farmers, and corn (maize) was the center of their farming.
At its peak, around 1100, Cahokia had perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people, probably a little more than London at the time.
Cahokia declined probably because of environmental damage, as cutting forests brought erosion and flooding; disease, climate change, social stress and warfare may also have played a part.

title: Cahokia's mounds
description: Cahokia's earthen mounds were built basket by basket; Monks Mound rises about 100 feet with a base like the Great Pyramid's and once held a large building, likely the seat of government; Woodhenge worked as a calendar.

facts.text: Cahokia's mounds were built of earth carried to the site basket by basket.
Monks Mound rises about 100 feet, its base is about the size of the Great Pyramid of Giza's, and it is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas.
A building about 100 feet long once stood on top of Monks Mound, believed to be the seat of Cahokia's government.
At Woodhenge, circles of wooden posts lined up with the rising sun at certain times of the year, so they served as a calendar.

title: Chaco's great houses
description: Ancestral Puebloans, ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples, built Chaco Canyon's multistory stone great houses from the mid-800s; Pueblo Bonito held over 600 rooms and roads linked Chaco to 150 great houses.

facts.text: The older name Anasazi comes from Navajo; Pueblo people consider it disrespectful and prefer Ancestral Puebloans.
In Chaco Canyon, in today's New Mexico, Chacoan culture flourished from the mid-800s for more than 300 years.
Chacoans built great houses: massive stone buildings of several stories with hundreds of rooms, often oriented to the sun, the moon and the cardinal directions.
Pueblo Bonito, the largest great house, was D-shaped, stood four to five stories tall and held over 600 rooms.
Roads linked Chaco Canyon's great houses to more than 150 great houses across the region.

title: Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings
description: At Mesa Verde the ancestors of Pueblo people built cliff dwellings in canyon alcoves from about 1180 to 1300, then moved south after the Great Drought; their descendants are today's Pueblo peoples.

facts.text: At Mesa Verde, in today's Colorado, the ancestors of Pueblo people built most of their cliff dwellings between about 1180 and 1300, in alcoves in the canyon walls.
Cliff Palace is the largest cliff dwelling in North America.
By 1300, after the Great Drought of 1276 to 1299, most people had left Mesa Verde, moving south into what is now New Mexico and Arizona.
The people of Mesa Verde are among the ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples.

title: The Great Law of Peace
description: The Peacemaker and Hiawatha joined the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca under the Great Law: 50 chiefs chosen by Clan Mothers, one vote per nation, unanimous decisions.

facts.text: Haudenosaunee means People of the Longhouse; the confederacy's five original nations were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca.
Haudenosaunee tradition credits the Peacemaker, helped by Hiawatha (Aionwatha), with founding the confederacy under the Great Law of Peace.
The Hiawatha Belt records how the five warring nations buried their weapons of war under the Tree of Peace, planted in Onondaga territory.
Wampum beads are made of white and purple shell, and the designs and colors of wampum belts are memory aids for history, traditions and laws.
Under the Great Law of Peace, 50 peace chiefs shared authority over civil affairs; each nation had one vote, and decisions had to be unanimous.
Each nation's chiefs are chosen by Clan Mothers.
After the Tuscarora joined in 1722, the confederacy became known to the English as the Six Nations.

Scholars disagree on when the confederacy formed: most place it in the mid to late 1400s, while Barbara Mann and Jerry Fields argue for 1142, the year of a solar eclipse that may match a sign in the sky in the oral tradition.

title: Did the League shape the Constitution?
description: Canassatego (1744) and Franklin (1751) linked the League to colonial union, and Congress acknowledged its contribution in 1988, but historians still argue how much it shaped the Constitution.

facts.text: At a 1744 treaty meeting, the Onondaga leader Canassatego urged the colonies to unite, and in 1751 Benjamin Franklin argued that if the Six Nations could form such a union, a dozen English colonies should manage one too.

In 1988, on the Constitution's 200th anniversary, Congress passed a resolution acknowledging the contribution of the Iroquois Confederacy and other Indian nations to the formation and development of the United States.
Historians argue over whether the confederacy influenced the Constitution; skeptics say European political theory supplied the Founders' models and the evidence for Native influence is thin.
The historians Donald Grinde and Bruce Johansen argue that Iroquois and other Native political ideas helped shape American government, including the Constitution.

title: What crossed the Atlantic
description: After 1492 American crops like corn, potatoes and tomatoes spread worldwide, while horses, cattle, pigs and wheat came to the Americas; horses transformed Plains bison hunting.

facts.text: The Columbian Exchange is the transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world that followed Columbus's voyage of 1492.
The name comes from the historian Alfred W. Crosby's 1972 book The Columbian Exchange, which sorted the exchange into diseases, animals and plants.
Farmers of the Americas gave the world corn (maize), potatoes, cassava and sweet potatoes, plus tomatoes, peanuts, squashes, pineapples and chili peppers.
Horses, pigs, cattle, goats and sheep adapted readily to the Americas, and wheat, rice, rye and barley prospered there too.
On horseback, Plains peoples could hunt bison far more successfully, boosting their food supplies until the 1870s, when the bison dwindled.

title: Epidemics in the Americas
description: The Americas had none of Eurasia's crowd diseases such as smallpox and measles, so Native peoples had no past exposure; populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650.

facts.text: Before 1492, the Americas had none of the acute infectious diseases, such as smallpox, measles and influenza, that had long troubled Eurasia and Africa; many came from herd animals like cattle and pigs, which the first Americans had not domesticated.
Across the Americas, populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650, largely because of epidemics.

title: Spain comes north
description: Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest continuously occupied European-founded US city, and colonized New Mexico from 1598, with Santa Fe as capital from 1610.

facts.text: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine, Florida, on September 8, 1565; it is the oldest continuously occupied city founded by Europeans in the United States.
Spain acted in Florida partly because France was trying to build permanent settlements there.
In 1598 Juan de Oñate led an expedition of settlers, priests and soldiers into today's New Mexico.
Santa Fe became the capital of Spanish New Mexico in 1610.

title: The Pueblo Revolt
description: After decades of religious persecution, forced labor and hunger, Po'pay coordinated the pueblos with knotted cords; on August 10, 1680 they rose and drove the Spanish out until 1692.

facts.text: Spanish missionaries forced Catholicism on the Pueblo peoples and burned their kivas, masks and other sacred objects, and Pueblo people suffered forced labor and hunger.
Po'pay, a religious leader from San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh), had been imprisoned and flogged by the Spanish before he planned the revolt.
Runners carried knotted cords to the pueblos; one knot was untied each day, and the revolt would begin when the last was untied.
On August 10, 1680, almost all the Pueblos rose together; by August 21 the Spanish had fled, leaving about 400 dead, including 21 priests.
The revolt forced the Spanish to retreat south to what is now El Paso, Texas.
The Pueblos stayed free until 1692, when Diego de Vargas retook New Mexico for Spain.

title: Jamestown barely survives
description: Jamestown (1607), the first permanent English settlement, sat on an unhealthy marshy site and nearly died in the Starving Time of 1609 to 1610.

facts.text: Jamestown, founded on May 14, 1607, by the Virginia Company of London, was the first permanent English settlement in North America.
Jamestown's marshy site proved unhealthy: bad river water, mosquitoes and short rations brought dysentery and fevers.
In the Starving Time, the winter of 1609 to 1610, drought, a Powhatan siege and scarce supplies left only about 60 of some 500 colonists alive.
In June 1610 the survivors boarded ships to go home, but an incoming fleet ordered them to turn back.

title: Tobacco makes Jamestown pay
description: John Rolfe's West Indies tobacco, first shipped in 1614, made the colony profitable and drove settlers onto Native land.

facts.text: John Rolfe replaced Virginia's harsh native tobacco with milder plants from the West Indies; after he shipped his first barrels to England in 1614, other colonists saw his lucrative results and copied him.
Profitable tobacco led settlers to press further into Native territory for rich new land.

title: The Powhatan chiefdom
description: Powhatan (Wahunsenacawh) ruled Tsenacomoco, dozens of tribes; peace came with Pocahontas's 1614 marriage to Rolfe, and war in 1622 when Opechancanough struck the spreading colony.

facts.text: Powhatan, whose given name was Wahunsenacawh, was paramount chief of Tsenacomoco in tidewater Virginia; he united dozens of tribes, more than 150 towns paid him tribute, and he was the highest authority in the region when the English built Jamestown.
John Rolfe married Powhatan's daughter Pocahontas in April 1614, and the marriage brought peace between the Powhatans and the English.
John Smith claimed that Pocahontas saved his life; some writers think he misunderstood a ceremony, and others say he invented the rescue.
In 1622 Powhatan warriors led by Opechancanough, Powhatan's brother and successor, struck the colony, killing 347 of about 1,200 English colonists.

title: Europeans enter a crowded continent
description: Spain and England built their first towns in lands already ruled by Native nations; St. Augustine was 42 years older than Jamestown, and epidemics reshaped the continent.

facts.text: St. Augustine, founded in 1565, is 42 years older than Jamestown, founded in 1607.
